chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: The planned excursion to Whitwell turned out quite differently from Elinor's expectations. She had prepared herself to be soaked, exhausted, and frightened. What happened was more unfortunate still: they did not go at all.

By ten o'clock everyone had gathered at the park for breakfast. Though rain had fallen all night, the morning looked fairly promising. Clouds were scattering across the sky, and the sun came out frequently. Everyone was cheerful and in excellent spirits, eager to enjoy themselves and determined to endure any amount of discomfort and hardship rather than fail to be happy.
The letters arrived while they were at breakfast. One was for Colonel Brandon. He took it, looked at the address, changed colour, and immediately went out of the room.
“What is wrong with Brandon?” Sir John asked.
Nobody could say.
“I hope he has not received bad news,” Lady Middleton said. “Something quite extraordinary must have happened to make Colonel Brandon leave my breakfast table so abruptly.”
About five minutes later, he came back.
“Nothing unfortunate in your letter, I hope, Colonel?” Mrs. Jennings asked the moment he entered.
“Nothing at all, ma'am. Thank you for asking.”
“Did it come from Avignon? I hope it does not say your sister has grown worse.”
“No, ma'am. It is from London, and concerns only a matter of business.”
“Then why did recognising the handwriting upset you so much, if it was merely business? Come, come, Colonel, that will not do. Let us hear what really happened.”
“My dear mother,” Lady Middleton said, “please consider what you are saying.”
“Perhaps it tells you your cousin Fanny has married?” Mrs. Jennings suggested, ignoring her daughter's rebuke.
“No, that is certainly not it.”
“Well then, Colonel, I know who sent it. And I hope she is quite well.”
“Who do you mean, ma'am?” he asked, colouring slightly.
“Oh! You know perfectly well whom I mean.”
“I am especially sorry, ma'am,” he said to Lady Middleton, “that this letter should have arrived today. The business it concerns requires me to go to London immediately.”
“To London!” Mrs. Jennings exclaimed. “What business can you possibly have there at this time of year?”
“I shall lose a great deal myself,” he continued, “by having to leave such pleasant company. But I regret it all the more because I fear you cannot gain admission to Whitwell without me.”
What a dreadful blow this was to everyone!
“But surely a note from you to the housekeeper would be enough, Mr. Brandon?” Marianne asked eagerly.
He shook his head in refusal.
“We must go,” Sir John said. “We cannot put it off when we have got this far. You must wait until tomorrow to go to London, Brandon. That is all.”
“I wish the matter could be settled so simply. But I cannot possibly postpone my journey for even a day!”
“If you would just tell us what the business is,” Mrs. Jennings said, “we could decide whether it might wait.”
“If you delayed leaving until we got back,” Willoughby said, “you would arrive less than six hours later.”
“I cannot spare even a single hour.”

Elinor then heard Willoughby say quietly to Marianne, “Some people cannot bear an outing arranged for pleasure. Brandon is one of them. I dare say he feared catching a cold and invented this trick to escape it. I would bet fifty guineas that he wrote the letter himself.”
“I do not doubt it at all,” Marianne answered.

“I have known you long enough, Brandon, to know that once you decide something, nobody can change your mind,” Sir John said. “Still, I hope you will think better of this. Consider the two Miss Careys, who have come over from Newton, and the three Miss Dashwoods, who have walked up from the cottage. Mr. Willoughby even rose two hours earlier than usual, all for the sake of going to Whitwell.”
Colonel Brandon again expressed his regret at causing the party such disappointment. At the same time, he insisted that there was no way to avoid it.
“Well then, when will you be coming back?”
“I hope we shall see you at Barton again,” Lady Middleton added, “as soon as you can conveniently leave London. We must postpone Whitwell until you return.”
“You are very kind. But I am so uncertain when I shall be able to return that I dare not make any promise about it.”
“Oh! He must come back, and he shall,” Sir John exclaimed. “If he is not here by the end of the week, I shall fetch him myself.”
“Yes, do that, Sir John,” Mrs. Jennings cried. “Perhaps then you will discover what his business really is.”
“I have no wish to pry into another man's affairs. I suppose it is something he is ashamed of.”
They were told that Colonel Brandon's horses were ready.
“Surely you are not riding all the way to London?” Sir John added.
“No, only to Honiton. From there I shall travel by post-chaise.”
“Well, since you insist on going, I wish you a pleasant journey. But you would do better to change your mind.”
“I assure you, I have no choice in the matter.”
He then said goodbye to everyone in the party.
“Is there any possibility of seeing you and your sisters in London this winter, Miss Dashwood?”
“I am afraid there is no possibility.”
“Then I must say goodbye for a longer time than I would have wished.”
To Marianne he only bowed, without saying a word.
“Come, Colonel,” Mrs. Jennings said, “before you leave, do tell us what you are going to do.”
He wished her good morning and left the room, with Sir John accompanying him.
Everyone now burst into the complaints and lamentations that politeness had so far restrained. Again and again they agreed how deeply annoying it was to have their hopes disappointed.
“All the same, I can guess his business,” Mrs. Jennings said triumphantly.
“Can you really, ma'am?” almost everyone asked.
“Yes. It concerns Miss Williams, I am certain of that.”
“And who exactly is Miss Williams?” Marianne asked.

“What! Do you not know who Miss Williams is? Surely you must have heard of her. She is a relation of the colonel's, my dear—a very close relation. We shall not say how close, in case we shock the young ladies.” Then, lowering her voice a little, she told Elinor, “She is his illegitimate daughter.”
“Really!”
“Oh yes, and as like him as anyone could be. I dare say the colonel will leave her everything he owns.”

When Sir John returned, he wholeheartedly joined the general regret at this unfortunate event. He ended by observing that, since they were all together, they must find some means of being happy. After discussion, they agreed that although happiness was possible only at Whitwell, driving through the countryside might produce a tolerable calmness of mind. The carriages were ordered. Willoughby's came first, and Marianne had never looked happier than when she stepped into it. He drove through the park at great speed, and they soon disappeared. Nobody saw them again until they returned, after everyone else had already come back. They both seemed delighted with their drive, but said only vaguely that they had stayed in the lanes while the others travelled over the downs.

They decided to dance that evening and to be extremely merry all day. More of the Careys came to dinner, giving them the pleasure of nearly twenty people around the table, a fact Sir John noted with great satisfaction. Willoughby sat in his usual place between the two elder Miss Dashwoods. Mrs. Jennings was on Elinor's right. Soon after they sat down, she leaned behind Elinor and Willoughby and said to Marianne, loudly enough for both to hear, “I have discovered you, for all your tricks. I know where you spent this morning.”
Marianne blushed and answered very quickly, “Where, may I ask?”
“Did you not know,” Willoughby asked, “that we went out in my curricle?”

“Yes, yes, Mr. Impudence, I know that perfectly well. And I was determined to discover where you had gone. I hope you like your house, Miss Marianne. I know it is a very large one. When I visit you, I hope you will have furnished it afresh, because it badly needed it when I was there six years ago.”

Marianne turned away in great embarrassment. Mrs. Jennings laughed heartily. Elinor learned that, determined to discover their destination, Mrs. Jennings had actually sent her maid to question Mr. Willoughby's groom. Through him she had found out that they had gone to Allenham and spent a considerable time walking around the garden and exploring the whole house.
Elinor could scarcely believe it. It seemed highly unlikely that Willoughby would suggest, or Marianne agree to, entering the house while Mrs. Smith was there, when Marianne had never met her.

As soon as they left the dining room, Elinor asked Marianne about it. To her great surprise, everything Mrs. Jennings had said proved entirely true. Marianne was quite angry that Elinor should doubt it.
“Why should you suppose, Elinor, that we did not go there or look through the house? Have you not often wanted to do exactly that yourself?”
“Yes, Marianne, but not while Mrs. Smith was at home, and not with Mr. Willoughby as my only companion.”
“But Mr. Willoughby is the only person entitled to show the house. And as we went in an open carriage, there was no room for another companion. I have never spent a more enjoyable morning.”
“I am afraid,” Elinor answered, “that enjoying an activity does not always prove it is a proper one.”

“On the contrary, Elinor, there could be no stronger proof. If there had been anything truly improper in my behaviour, I should have felt it at the time. We always know when we are doing wrong. If I had felt that conviction, I could not have enjoyed myself.”
“But my dear Marianne, now that it has exposed you to some very impertinent comments, do you not begin to question whether your behaviour was wise?”

“If Mrs. Jennings's impertinent comments prove improper behaviour, then we are all doing wrong every moment of our lives. I care no more for her criticism than I would for her praise. I do not feel that I did anything wrong by walking through Mrs. Smith's grounds or looking at her house. They will belong to Mr. Willoughby one day, and—”
“Even if they were going to belong to you one day, Marianne, that would not justify what you have done.”

She blushed at the suggestion, but was visibly pleased by it. After ten minutes of serious thought, she returned to her sister and said with great good humour, “Perhaps, Elinor, going to Allenham was rather unwise of me. But Mr. Willoughby was particularly eager to show it to me, and I assure you it is a charming house. There is an especially pretty sitting room upstairs, a comfortable size for everyday use. With modern furniture it would be delightful. It is a corner room with windows on two sides. From one side you look across the bowling green behind the house to a beautiful wood on the hillside. From the other, you see the church and village, with those magnificent steep hills we have so often admired beyond them. I did not see it at its best: nothing could look more dismal than the furniture. But if it were fitted out afresh—Willoughby says a couple of hundred pounds would make it one of the pleasantest summer rooms in England.”
If the others had not interrupted Elinor's listening, Marianne would have gone on to describe every room in the house with just as much delight.

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: Colonel Brandon's sudden departure from the park, and his firmness in concealing the reason, occupied Mrs. Jennings's thoughts and excited her curiosity for two or three days. She was much given to wondering, as anyone must be who takes a lively interest in every arrival and departure among their acquaintances. Almost without pause, she wondered what could explain it. Certain he had received bad news, she considered every possible misfortune that might have struck him, firmly determined that he should not escape them all.

“Something very distressing must have happened, I am sure,” she said. “I could see it in his face. Poor man! I fear his finances may be in trouble. Delaford was never thought to bring in more than two thousand a year, and his brother left everything dreadfully encumbered with debt. I really believe he was sent for over money. What else could it be? I wonder whether that is it. I would give anything to know the truth. Perhaps it concerns Miss Williams. Indeed, now I think of it, I dare say it does, because he looked so self-conscious when I mentioned her. She may be ill in London. Nothing could be more likely; I have the impression that she is always rather sickly. I would bet anything that it is about Miss Williams. He is hardly likely to have financial difficulties now, being such a prudent man. Surely he must have cleared the estate's debts by this time. I wonder what it can be! Perhaps his sister in Avignon is worse and has sent for him to come over. His rushing off like that certainly suggests it. Well, with all my heart I wish him free of every trouble—and a good wife into the bargain.”

So Mrs. Jennings wondered and talked. Each new guess changed her opinion, and every possibility seemed equally likely as it arose. Elinor genuinely cared about Colonel Brandon's welfare, but could not feel all the amazement at his sudden departure that Mrs. Jennings wanted from her. In her view, the event did not justify such prolonged astonishment or such varied speculation. Besides, her capacity for wondering was occupied elsewhere. She could not understand her sister and Willoughby's extraordinary silence about a subject they must know interested the whole family deeply. Every day that the silence continued made it seem stranger and less compatible with either of their characters. Elinor could not imagine why they failed to acknowledge openly to her mother and herself what their constant behaviour towards each other declared had happened.

She could easily understand that they might be unable to marry at once. Willoughby was independent, but there was no reason to suppose him wealthy. Sir John estimated his estate's income at six or seven hundred pounds a year, yet he lived in a manner that such an income could scarcely support, and often complained of his poverty himself. But Elinor could not explain this peculiar secrecy about their engagement, which in fact concealed nothing. It so completely contradicted their usual opinions and conduct that she sometimes wondered whether they were really engaged at all. That doubt was enough to keep her from questioning Marianne.

Nothing could have shown greater attachment to the whole family than Willoughby's behaviour. Towards Marianne he displayed all the special tenderness of a lover; towards the others, the affectionate attention of a son and brother. He seemed to regard and love the cottage as his own home, spending far more time there than at Allenham. Unless a general engagement brought them together at the park, his morning exercise almost always ended at the cottage. He would spend the rest of the day beside Marianne, with his favourite pointer at her feet.

One evening, about a week after Colonel Brandon left the neighbourhood, Willoughby's heart seemed more open than usual to affection for everything around him. When Mrs. Dashwood happened to mention her plan to improve the cottage in spring, he passionately opposed any alteration to a place that love had made perfect in his eyes.
“What!” he exclaimed. “Improve this dear cottage! No, I shall never agree to that. If you care at all for my feelings, you must not add a single stone to its walls or an inch to its size.”
“Do not be alarmed,” Miss Dashwood said. “Nothing of the sort will happen. My mother will never have enough money to undertake it.”
“I am sincerely glad to hear it,” he exclaimed. “May she always remain poor if she can find no better use for riches.”

“Thank you, Willoughby. But you may be certain that all the improvements in the world would not persuade me to sacrifice your affection for a place, or that of anyone I love. Whatever money I have left unused when I settle my accounts in spring, I would rather leave it lying idle than spend it in a way that causes you pain. You may depend on that. But are you really so fond of this place that you can find no fault with it?”

“I am,” he replied. “It is faultless to me. More than that: I consider it the only kind of building in which happiness is possible. If I were rich enough, I would pull down Combe immediately and rebuild it to match this cottage exactly.”
“With a dark, narrow staircase and a smoky kitchen, I suppose,” Elinor said.

“Yes,” he cried, just as eagerly, “with every single thing that belongs to it. There should not be the slightest difference in any of its conveniences or inconveniences. Then, and only then, beneath such a roof, I might perhaps be as happy at Combe as I have been at Barton.”
“I flatter myself,” Elinor answered, “that even with the disadvantages of better rooms and a wider staircase, you may one day find your own house as faultless as you now find this one.”
“There are certainly circumstances,” Willoughby said, “that could make it much dearer to me. But this place will always have one claim on my affection that no other place can possibly share.”
Mrs. Dashwood looked happily at Marianne. The expression in her beautiful eyes, fixed on Willoughby, made it quite clear how fully she understood him.

“How often I wished, when I was at Allenham this time last year, that someone lived in Barton Cottage!” he continued. “I never came within sight of it without admiring its situation and regretting that it stood empty. How little I imagined that when I next came to the neighbourhood, the very first news Mrs. Smith would give me was that the cottage had been taken. I immediately felt a pleasure and interest in that news which only some foreknowledge of the happiness it would bring me can explain. Surely that must have been it, Marianne?” He lowered his voice to address her. Then, returning to his previous tone, he said, “And yet, Mrs. Dashwood, you would spoil this house? You would rob it of its simplicity with supposed improvements! You would turn this dear parlour, where our acquaintance began and where we have since spent so many happy hours together, into an ordinary entrance hall. Everyone would hurry through the very room that has so far offered more real comfort and convenience than any room of the grandest proportions in the world could possibly provide.”
Mrs. Dashwood assured him again that she would attempt no alteration of that kind.

“You are a good woman,” he replied warmly. “Your promise puts my mind at rest. Take it a little further, and you will make me happy. Promise that not only the house will stay the same, but that I shall always find you and your family as unchanged as your home. Promise you will always treat me with the kindness that has made everything connected with you so dear to me.”
She readily gave the promise. Throughout the rest of the evening, Willoughby's behaviour showed both his affection and his happiness.
“Shall we see you at dinner tomorrow?” Mrs. Dashwood asked as he was leaving. “I will not invite you for the morning, because we must walk to the park to call on Lady Middleton.”
He promised to arrive at the cottage by four o'clock.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: Mrs. Dashwood called on Lady Middleton the next day, taking two of her daughters with her. Marianne excused herself on some slight pretext of work to be done. Her mother assumed that Willoughby had promised the previous evening to visit while the others were out, and was perfectly happy for her to stay at home.

On returning from the park, they found Willoughby's curricle and servant waiting outside the cottage. Mrs. Dashwood felt certain her guess had been correct. So far, everything was as she had expected. But inside the house she encountered something no foresight had prepared her for. They had scarcely entered the passage when Marianne hurried out of the parlour in obvious distress, holding a handkerchief to her eyes. Without acknowledging them, she ran upstairs. Surprised and alarmed, they went straight into the room she had left. Willoughby was there alone, leaning against the mantelpiece with his back to them. He turned as they entered, and his face showed that he shared much of the emotion that had overwhelmed Marianne.
“What is wrong with her?” Mrs. Dashwood exclaimed as she entered. “Is she unwell?”
“I hope not,” he answered, attempting to look cheerful. Then, with a forced smile, he added, “It is I who have more reason to expect to be ill. I am suffering a very great disappointment!”
“A disappointment?”

“Yes. I cannot keep my engagement with you. This morning Mrs. Smith has used the privilege of wealth to send a poor dependent cousin to London on business. I have just received my instructions and said goodbye at Allenham. Now, to cheer myself up, I have come to say goodbye to you.”
“To London! Are you leaving this very morning?”
“Almost at this very moment.”
“How unfortunate. Still, Mrs. Smith must be obliged. I hope her business will not keep you away from us for long.”
He reddened as he answered, “You are very kind, but I do not expect to return to Devonshire soon. I never visit Mrs. Smith more than once within a year.”
“And is Mrs. Smith your only friend? Is Allenham the only house nearby where you would be welcome? For shame, Willoughby! Surely you do not wait to be invited here?”
He grew still redder. Looking down at the floor, he answered only, “You are much too kind.”
Mrs. Dashwood looked at Elinor in surprise. Elinor was equally astonished. For a few moments nobody spoke. Mrs. Dashwood was the first to break the silence.

“I can only add, my dear Willoughby, that you will always be welcome at Barton Cottage. I shall not urge you to return immediately, since only you can judge how far that would please Mrs. Smith. On that point, I am no more inclined to question your judgment than to doubt your wishes.”
“My present commitments,” Willoughby replied in confusion, “are of a kind that—that I dare not hope—”

He broke off. Mrs. Dashwood was too astonished to answer, and another silence followed. Willoughby ended it with a faint smile. “It is foolish to linger like this. I will not torment myself any further by staying among friends whose company I cannot now enjoy.”
He hurriedly said goodbye to them all and left the room. They watched him get into his carriage, and within a minute it had disappeared from sight.
Mrs. Dashwood was too overcome to speak. She immediately left the parlour to give way in private to the distress and alarm his abrupt departure had caused.

Elinor was at least as uneasy as her mother. She considered what had just happened with anxiety and suspicion. Willoughby's manner at parting, his embarrassment and pretended cheerfulness, and above all his reluctance to accept her mother's invitation disturbed her deeply. That hesitation was so unlike a lover, so unlike himself. One moment she feared he had never intended anything serious; the next, that some unhappy quarrel had taken place between him and Marianne. A serious quarrel would most readily explain the distress in which her sister had left the room. Yet when Elinor considered the strength of Marianne's love, a quarrel seemed almost impossible.

Whatever the details of their parting, there could be no doubt of her sister's suffering. Elinor thought with the tenderest compassion of the violent grief Marianne was probably not only yielding to for relief, but nurturing and encouraging as a duty.
About half an hour later, her mother returned. Her eyes were red, but her expression was not without cheerfulness.
“Our dear Willoughby must be several miles from Barton by now, Elinor,” she said, sitting down to her sewing. “And how heavy his heart must be as he travels!”

“It is all so strange. To leave so suddenly! It seems to have happened in an instant. Only last night he was here, so happy, cheerful, and affectionate. And now, with barely ten minutes' warning—gone, and with no intention of returning! Something more must have happened than he admitted. He neither spoke nor behaved like himself. You must have noticed the difference as clearly as I did. What can explain it? Could they have quarrelled? Why else was he so unwilling to accept your invitation?”

“He did not lack the wish to accept, Elinor. I could see that plainly. He was not able to do so. I assure you, I have considered it all, and can explain perfectly everything that seemed strange to me at first, just as it did to you.”
“Can you really explain it!”

“Yes. I have found a thoroughly satisfactory explanation. But you, Elinor, like to doubt wherever possible. I know it will not satisfy you; still, you will not persuade me to give up my confidence in it. I am convinced Mrs. Smith suspects his love for Marianne and disapproves, perhaps because she has other plans for him. That is why she wants him away. The business she has sent him to conduct is merely an excuse to dismiss him. That is what I believe has happened. He also knows that she disapproves of the connection, and therefore dare not tell her at present that he is engaged to Marianne. Because he depends on her, he feels obliged to submit to her plans and stay away from Devonshire for a time. You will tell me, I know, that this may or may not be what happened. But I shall hear no objections unless you can offer another explanation as satisfactory as this one. Now, Elinor, what do you say?”
“Nothing. You have already supplied the answer I would have given.”

“So you would have said it may or may not have happened. Oh, Elinor, I cannot understand your feelings! You would rather believe evil without proof than good. You would rather look for misery for Marianne and guilt in poor Willoughby than find an excuse for him. You are determined to blame him because his farewell was less affectionate than his usual behaviour. Will you make no allowance for thoughtlessness, or for spirits lowered by a recent disappointment? Must we reject probabilities simply because they are not certainties? Do we owe nothing to a man we have every reason to love and no reason in the world to mistrust? Nothing to the possibility of motives perfectly defensible in themselves, although necessarily secret for a while? And after all, what do you suspect him of?”

“I can scarcely tell you myself. But when someone changes as much as we have just seen him change, suspicion of something unpleasant is inevitable. Still, there is a great deal of truth in what you say about making allowances for him. I wish to judge everyone fairly. Willoughby may certainly have very good reasons for his behaviour, and I shall hope he has. But it would have been more like him to admit them openly. Secrecy may be wise; nevertheless, I cannot help wondering at his being the one to practise it.”
“Then do not blame him for acting against his nature when it is necessary. But you really do admit that what I have said in his defence is fair? I am happy, then, and he is acquitted.”

“Not completely. It may be wise to hide their engagement—if they are engaged—from Mrs. Smith. If so, Willoughby may have very good reason to spend little time in Devonshire just now. But that does not excuse their hiding it from us.”
“Hiding it from us! My dear child, are you accusing Willoughby and Marianne of concealment? How very strange, when every day your looks have reproached them for being too open.”
“I need no proof that they love each other,” Elinor said. “But I do need proof of their engagement.”
“I am entirely satisfied on both points.”
“Yet neither of them has said a single word to you about being engaged.”

“I have needed no words when their actions have spoken so clearly. For at least the past fortnight, has his behaviour to Marianne and to all of us not shown that he loves her and regards her as his future wife? Has he not shown us the affection of the closest relation? Have we not understood each other perfectly? Have his looks, his manner, his attentive and affectionate respect not asked for my consent every day? My Elinor, how can you doubt their engagement? How could the thought even enter your mind? Willoughby must be certain of your sister's love. How can you imagine him leaving her, perhaps for months, without telling her of his own affection? How could they part without confiding in each other?”

“I admit,” Elinor replied, “that everything except one circumstance supports their being engaged. But that one circumstance is their complete silence about it, and to me it nearly outweighs all the others.”

“How strange! You must think very badly of Willoughby if, after everything we have openly witnessed between them, you can doubt the nature of their relationship. Has he been acting a part towards your sister all this time? Do you really suppose he feels nothing for her?”
“No, I cannot believe that. He must love her, and I am sure he does.”
“Then it is a peculiar sort of love, if he can leave her with the indifference and disregard for the future that you attribute to him.”

“You must remember, my dear mother, that I have never treated this as certain. I admit I have had doubts, but they are weaker now and may soon disappear entirely. If we find that they write to one another, all my fears will be removed.”

“What an immense concession! If you saw them at the altar, you would suppose they were about to be married. Ungenerous girl! I need no such proof. In my opinion, nothing has happened to justify doubt. They have attempted no secrecy; everything has been consistently open and unreserved. You cannot question your sister's wishes, so it must be Willoughby you suspect. But why? Is he not a man of honour and feeling? Has he behaved inconsistently in any way that gives cause for alarm? Could he be deceitful?”

“I hope not; I believe not,” Elinor exclaimed. “I love Willoughby, truly love him. Doubting his honesty cannot hurt you more than it hurts me. The suspicion came without my wishing it, and I shall not encourage it. I admit the change in his manner this morning startled me. He did not speak like himself, or answer your kindness with any warmth. But the circumstances you imagine could explain it all. He had just parted from my sister and seen her leave him in terrible distress. If fear of offending Mrs. Smith obliged him to resist the temptation of returning soon, while he knew that refusing your invitation and announcing a long absence would make his conduct towards our family seem ungenerous and suspicious, he might understandably be embarrassed and troubled. In that case, I think a clear, honest admission of his difficulties would have done him more credit and better suited his usual character. But I will not criticise someone's conduct on so ungenerous a basis as their judging differently from me, or departing from what I consider right and consistent.”

“You speak very properly. Willoughby certainly does not deserve suspicion. We have not known him long, but he is no stranger in this neighbourhood. Who has ever said anything against him? If he were free to act independently and marry at once, leaving without openly acknowledging everything to me might have been odd. But he is not. In some ways the engagement has begun under difficult circumstances, since the date of their marriage must be very uncertain. Even secrecy, so far as it can be preserved, may now be extremely wise.”

Margaret's arrival interrupted their conversation, leaving Elinor free to think over all the explanations her mother had offered, acknowledge how probable many of them were, and hope that every one was correct.

They did not see Marianne until dinner. She entered and took her seat without a word. Her eyes were red and swollen, and even then she seemed scarcely able to hold back her tears. She avoided everyone's gaze and could neither eat nor speak. After a while her mother silently pressed her hand with tender sympathy. What little firmness Marianne had gave way entirely; she burst into tears and left the room.

This overwhelming misery lasted all evening. She had no power to control herself because she had no wish to do so. The smallest reference to anything connected with Willoughby instantly overcame her. Her family attended anxiously to her comfort, but unless they remained completely silent, they could not avoid every subject her feelings linked with him.

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Marianne would have thought herself quite unforgivable if she had managed any sleep on the first night after parting from Willoughby. She would have been ashamed to face her family the next morning unless she rose needing rest even more than when she lay down. But the very feelings that made such calmness disgraceful left her in no danger of achieving it. She stayed awake all night and cried through most of it. She got up with a headache, unable to talk and unwilling to eat anything. Every moment brought fresh distress to her mother and sisters, while she rejected any attempt from them to comfort her. Her emotional sensitivity was powerful enough!
After breakfast she went out alone and wandered around Allenham village. For most of the morning she dwelt on memories of past pleasure and wept over the change in her present circumstances.

She spent the evening indulging her feelings in the same way. She played every favourite song she used to perform for Willoughby, every tune they had most often sung together. She sat at the instrument studying every line of music he had copied for her, until her heart was so heavy that she could make herself no sadder. Every day she fed her grief in this way. Whole hours passed at the pianoforte as she alternated singing and crying, her tears often stopping her voice completely. In books, as in music, she sought out the misery that comparing the past with the present was certain to produce. She read only what they had once read together.

Such intense suffering could not last for ever. Within a few days it subsided into a quieter melancholy. Yet her daily return to these occupations, her solitary walks and silent reflections, still brought occasional outpourings of grief as intense as before.

No letter arrived from Willoughby, and Marianne seemed to expect none. Her mother was surprised, and Elinor grew uneasy again. But Mrs. Dashwood could always find an explanation when she wanted one, and it would at least satisfy herself.

“Remember, Elinor,” she said, “how often Sir John collects our letters from the post himself and takes ours there. We have agreed that secrecy may be necessary. We must admit that it would be impossible to preserve it if their letters passed through Sir John's hands.”

Elinor could not deny this and tried to accept it as a sufficient reason for their silence. But there was one way to learn the truth and clear up the mystery immediately that seemed to her so direct, so simple, and so suitable that she could not help proposing it to her mother.

“Why not simply ask Marianne,” she said, “whether or not she is engaged to Willoughby? Coming from you, her mother—and so kind and indulgent a mother—the question could not offend her. It would follow naturally from your love for her. She used to be entirely open, especially with you.”

“I would not ask that question for anything in the world. Suppose it were possible they were not engaged: what suffering the question would cause! In any case, it would be most ungenerous. I should never deserve her confidence again if I forced her to confess something she means for now to acknowledge to nobody. I know Marianne's heart. I know she loves me dearly, and I shall not be the last to hear when circumstances make it suitable to tell us. I would never try to force anyone's confidence, least of all a child's. A sense of duty might prevent her from refusing, even when she wished to.”

Considering her sister's youth, Elinor thought this generosity excessive. She pressed the point further, but without success. Common sense, ordinary care, and simple prudence were all submerged in Mrs. Dashwood's romantic sensitivity.

Several days passed before anyone in the family mentioned Willoughby's name in front of Marianne. Sir John and Mrs. Jennings were less delicate: their jokes added pain to many an already painful hour. But one evening Mrs. Dashwood happened to pick up a volume of Shakespeare and exclaimed:
“We never finished Hamlet, Marianne. Our dear Willoughby left before we could read it all. We shall put it aside until he returns… Though perhaps that may not happen for months.”
“Months!” Marianne exclaimed in great surprise. “No—not even many weeks.”
Mrs. Dashwood regretted her remark. Elinor, however, was pleased: it had prompted an answer from Marianne that showed such confidence in Willoughby and such knowledge of his intentions.

One morning, about a week after he left the neighbourhood, Marianne was persuaded to join her sisters on their usual walk instead of wandering alone. Until then she had carefully avoided all company on her outings. If her sisters planned to walk on the downs, she immediately slipped away towards the lanes. If they spoke of the valley, she was just as quick to climb the hills, and could never be found when the others set out. At last Elinor, who strongly disapproved of her continual isolation, managed to secure her company. They followed the road through the valley, mostly in silence. Marianne's thoughts could not be controlled, and Elinor, satisfied with one success, attempted nothing further for the moment. Beyond the valley's entrance, the landscape remained fertile but became less wild and more open. A long stretch of the road along which they had first travelled to Barton came into view. On reaching it they stopped to look around. From this spot, which none of their previous walks had happened to reach, they could examine the landscape that formed the distant view from their cottage.

Among the things before them, they soon noticed something moving: a man on horseback riding towards them. In a few minutes they could tell he was a gentleman. A moment later, Marianne cried out in delight:
“It is him! It really is! I know it is!” She was hurrying to meet him when Elinor called:
“Marianne, I really think you are mistaken. That is not Willoughby. The man is not tall enough, and he does not carry himself in the same way.”
“He does, he does!” Marianne cried. “I am certain of it. His manner, his coat, his horse! I knew he would return so soon.”

As she spoke she hurried forward. Almost certain it was not Willoughby, Elinor quickened her own pace and kept beside her, hoping to prevent Marianne's behaviour from attracting particular notice. They soon came within thirty yards of the gentleman. Marianne looked again, and her heart sank. She turned abruptly and was hurrying back when both sisters called out for her to stay. A third voice, almost as familiar as Willoughby's, joined theirs in asking her to stop. She turned in surprise, recognised Edward Ferrars, and welcomed him.

He was the only person in the world she could forgive at that moment for not being Willoughby, the only one who could have won a smile from her. But she cleared her tears away to smile at him, and for a time forgot her disappointment in her sister's happiness.
He got down from his horse, handed it to his servant, and walked back with them to Barton. Visiting them had been the purpose of his journey.

They all welcomed him warmly, especially Marianne, who showed even more affection in her greeting than Elinor herself. To Marianne, the meeting between Edward and her sister seemed merely a continuation of the inexplicable coldness she had so often noticed between them at Norland. Edward in particular showed none of the looks or words a lover ought to offer on such an occasion. He was awkward, seemed barely pleased to see them, and looked neither delighted nor cheerful. He said little unless questions forced him to speak, and gave Elinor no special sign of affection. Marianne watched and listened with growing astonishment. She almost began to dislike Edward. As every feeling did with her, it ended by carrying her thoughts back to Willoughby, whose manners formed a striking contrast to those of his intended brother-in-law.
After the first surprise and questions of their meeting, a brief silence followed. Marianne then asked whether Edward had come straight from London. No, he had been in Devonshire for a fortnight.
“A fortnight!” she repeated, astonished that he had spent so long in the same county as Elinor without seeing her.
He looked rather troubled as he added that he had been staying with friends near Plymouth.
“Have you visited Sussex recently?” Elinor asked him.
“I stayed at Norland around a month ago.”
“And what does dear, dear Norland look like?” Marianne exclaimed.
“Dear, dear Norland,” Elinor said, “probably looks much as it usually does at this season. The woods and paths will be thick with fallen leaves.”

“Oh,” Marianne cried, “how thrilling it used to be to watch them fall! What delight I took in walking while the wind swept them in showers around me! What feelings they inspired, together with the season and the air! Now nobody cares to look at them. They are only a nuisance, hastily swept away and removed from sight as much as possible.”
“Not everyone,” Elinor said, “shares your passionate love of dead leaves.”

“No. My feelings are seldom shared, seldom understood. But sometimes they are.” She fell into thought for a few moments, then roused herself. “Now, Edward,” she said, drawing his attention to the view, “there is Barton Valley. Look up at it and remain calm if you can. Look at those hills! Have you ever seen their equal? On the left, among those woods and plantations, is Barton Park. You can see one end of the house. And there, beneath that farthest hill, rising so magnificently, is our cottage.”
“It is beautiful countryside,” he answered. “But these low-lying places must get very muddy in winter.”
“How can you think about mud with such sights before you?”
“Because,” he replied, smiling, “among the other things before me, I can see a very muddy lane.”
“How strange!” Marianne said to herself, continuing along the road.
“Do you have pleasant neighbours here? Are the Middletons agreeable people?”
“No, not all of them,” Marianne replied. “We could hardly have been less fortunate in our situation.”

“Marianne!” her sister exclaimed. “How can you say that? How can you be so unfair? They are a very respectable family, Mr. Ferrars, and have treated us with the greatest friendliness. Have you forgotten, Marianne, how many pleasant days we owe to them?”
“No,” Marianne answered quietly, “nor how many painful moments we owe them.”

Elinor ignored this. Turning her attention to their visitor, she tried to maintain something like a conversation by discussing their new home and its conveniences, drawing an occasional question or remark from him. His coldness and reserve hurt her deeply. She was vexed and half angry. But she decided to let his past behaviour, rather than his present manner, guide her own. She showed no resentment or displeasure, and treated him as she thought their family connection required.
